title: How People Really Choose a Face Cream
metaTitle: How People Really Choose a Face Cream: Natural vs Certified
description: Natural, organic or certified? Find out what you can actually verify about a face cream and how independent certification helps you choose with confidence.
bodyHtml:
Choosing a face cream sounds simple.

Walk into a beauty shop, open an online store or search for “natural face cream” and you will quickly find dozens of products competing for your attention.

Natural. Organic. Vegan. Botanical. Clean. Dermatologically tested. Sustainable.

Then come the ingredients, the packaging, the reviews, the price and the claims on the label.

So how do you decide?

There is no single answer. But when choosing a natural or organic cosmetic, there is one question that can make the process much clearer:

What can you actually verify about the product?

Start with what you are looking for

Before looking at labels or certifications, the first step is surprisingly practical: what do you actually need from the product?

A face cream can be designed for different purposes and skin needs. Texture, ingredients, fragrance, formulation, intended use and price can all influence whether a particular product is right for you.

This is why there is no universally “best” face cream.

The right choice depends on the individual consumer and on what they are looking for.

But once you have narrowed down the type of product you want, another question becomes important:

How do you assess the claims made about it?

Natural does not automatically mean certified

One of the challenges of shopping for natural cosmetics is that the words used on packaging can be difficult to interpret.

In the European Union, there is currently no harmonised legal definition specifically establishing what a cosmetic product must be in order to be called “natural” or “organic”. These terms are treated as cosmetic claims and are subject to common criteria designed to ensure that claims are verifiable and not misleading. However, there is no mandatory harmonised certification scheme specifically for natural and organic cosmetics. (NATRUE)

That means that seeing the word “natural” on a product does not, by itself, tell you that the product has been certified against a particular natural cosmetics standard.

Since 27 September 2026, new EU rules on environmental claims and sustainability labels apply across the EU (Directive (EU) 2024/825, known as the ECGT Directive). Vague environmental claims such as “eco-friendly” or “green” are no longer allowed unless they are specified and substantiated, and sustainability labels must be based on an independent certification scheme or established by public authorities. Even a word like “natural” may need to be anchored in something specific, such as certified content or a defined criterion, when it suggests an environmental benefit. (NATRUE)

This is where voluntary certification schemes can become useful.

What does a certification label actually tell you?

A certification label is different from a marketing description.

NATRUE is a private, voluntary and international standard for natural and organic cosmetics. Its criteria establish requirements concerning ingredients, their origin and processing, formulation and other aspects of certified products. (NATRUE)

NATRUE does not directly certify the products itself. Instead, products seeking certification are assessed by independent certification bodies approved by NATRUE. (NATRUE)

For consumers, that distinction matters.

The value of a certification label is not simply the word printed next to the product. It is the standard and verification process behind it.

Look beyond the front of the packaging

The front of a cosmetic product is designed to communicate quickly.

The back and the product information are where you can usually find more detail.

For a consumer interested in natural or organic cosmetics, a useful approach is to look at:

The product’s ingredients list.

The claims made by the brand.

Whether the product carries a recognised certification label.

What that certification actually requires.

Whether the certification can be independently verified.

NATRUE, for example, maintains a public database where consumers can search for certified products and raw materials carrying the NATRUE label. (NATRUE)

That gives consumers another way to move from a claim on a package to information about the standard behind it.

Why certification can make information easier to understand

Imagine two products.

Both describe themselves as natural.

With the first product, you only have the brand’s own description.

With the second, the product also carries a recognised certification label. You can then investigate the criteria behind that label and the verification process used to assess the product.

The certification does not tell you whether you will personally like the cream.

It does not tell you whether its texture will suit your skin.

And it does not replace reading the ingredients or understanding the product.

What it can do is provide an additional reference point for evaluating the natural or organic claims being made.

Price is still part of the decision

Certification is only one part of a purchasing decision.

Price matters. So do formulation, texture, fragrance, brand reputation, availability and personal preferences.

For a consumer, the goal is not to find a label that makes every other consideration irrelevant.

It is to have enough reliable information to make an informed choice.

That is particularly relevant when comparing independent natural and organic cosmetics, where products can differ significantly in formulation, positioning and price.

A simple way to think about it

When choosing a face cream, you can think about the decision in three layers:

First: Does the product meet my personal needs?

Second: Do I understand what the brand is claiming?

Third: Is there evidence or independent verification behind the claims that matter to me?

There is no single formula for choosing a cosmetic product.

But learning to distinguish between a marketing claim and a defined certification standard can make the process much easier.

For natural and organic cosmetics, that distinction is especially useful.

Because sometimes the most important question is not simply:

“What does this product say it is?”

It is:

“What stands behind that claim?”
